newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian stocks mixed, market to stay weak.
newsitem.headline: Croatian stocks mixed, market to stay weak.

text.p: Croatian stocks closed mixed on Thursday ahead of the public holiday, with Zagrebacka Banka forging ahead on stronger volume.
But traders expected the market to remain weak amid little buying interest for most issues after poorer than expected 1996 results for some of the most actively traded companies.
"I can't foresee any important changes... Investors are obviously scrutinising the firms' annual results and this has knocked down the prices," said Marko Nikolac of Metroholding brokerage.

But he said this did not apply to fully-listed Zagrebacka and drugs firm Pliva. Their prices, apart from good performance last year, also reflected the trade in their 1/10 and 1/5 respective Global Depository Receipts (GDRs) in London.
With 3,875 shares sold, Zagrebacka was the most active issue on Thursday. It firmed 50 kuna, recouping some of its recent losses to end the week at 2,100 kuna.
"Something must be happening...Some kind of information favourable for the bank must have been leaked to investors because they are buying larger quantities at a higher price," Nikolac said.

After the Zagreb bourse closed, the bank announced it was about to reach a deal with foreign creditors on a loan for at least 300 million German marks. This has caused its GDRs to rise strongly since to $35.75 each from $34.12 at the open.
Pliva remained unchanged at 440 kuna, selling 878 shares.

Fully-listed Varazdinska Banka B-series bearer shares led decliners, falling 10 percent to 200 kuna on volume of 50 in a first deal after this week's 5-for-1 split. The bank's A-series ordinaries lost 10 kuna to 250 on volume of 368 shares.
Seven of 17 active issues rose, six fell and four were flat. Volume rose to 8,828 shares, turnover was almost four times higher at 10.4 million kuna.
Weekly turnover was a little higher at 25.3 million kuna.
Biggest gainer hotelier Laguna climbed 150 kuna to 1,350 -- still below its recent average of around 1,400 -- with 142 shares sold.
Food processor Podravka, which sets the trend for stocks in a semi-regulated segment, reversed its downward trend by inching up five kuna to 260 on volume of 1,544 shares.
"Rumours that Podravka had a huge loss must have disappointed foreign buyers who were buying it 'en masse'," Nikolac said.
But a company source said earlier this week the loss was mostly due to five subsidiaries Podravka had sold late in 1996.
"If that's so, it can in the long-term bring growth," Nikolac said, adding it was unlikely to fall below 245-250 kuna again.
